LESSON MENU
TIMER & COUNTER INSTRUCTIONSNS
Timer and counter instructions are very powerful and can be used for a variety of operations. We will look at the details, requirements, and operation of both types of instructions.
DISCUSSION

The table below shows the different timer and counting instructions. Let's start by looking at the timer instructions. The reset instruction is used by both types of instructions and will be covered last...

There are three different timer instructions: Timer On-Delay, Timer Off-Delay, and the Retentive Timer. Before looking at the operation of these instructions, let's look at the parameters and information these instructions require or provide...

Timers require memory to operate. In the PLC's memory, all information is organized in data files. Data files contain three sixteen-bit words as shown below. Depending on the PLC you use, the arrangement of the information may be different...

The first word contains three bits. These bits can be accessed using the bit instructions. The bits include: the timer enable (EN), time timing (TT), and timer done (DN). These bits can tell you exactly what the timer is doing...
The rest of the bits for this word are used by the PLC itself and are not available for use or test.
The next word is the preset value. This the value you want the counter to reach before stopping. The value must be specified during the programming process.
The last word is the accumulator value. This is the current value of the timer. Since there may be many different timers operating at the same time, each one has to remember its own current values...

When the timer instruction is performed, it places its accumulator value in the PLC microprocessor's accumulator, summing the two values. The microprocessor's accumulator contained the elapsed time intervals that passed since the instruction was performed...

The timer then copies the new accumulator value and stores it in the data file. If the new accumulator value is equal to or greater than the preset value, the timer stops, setting the timing bit to low and the done bit to high.............

It is important to note that the accumulator value does not actually represent any particular time. Rather, the value represents the number of intervals that have elapsed for a given amount of time...

The time interval is known as a time base. On many PLCs, the time base can be changed to different values, like 1 second, 0.1 second, 0.01 second, and so on. To figure out the elapsed time, multiply the time base by the accumulator value...
The example below shows how to determine preset values and accumulator values in time, given a particular time base.
The accumulator's starting value can be user-specified. Typically, the accumulator starts at zero.

Many PLC systems reserve a section of memory for timer data files. Remember, in our example, timer data files are three words of 16 bits each. Only the EN, TT, and DN bits can be accessed using the bit instructions...

Now that we have looked at the general guidelines of all timing instructions, let's look at the individual timing instructions shown below. The first instruction is the Timer On-Delay (TON) instruction...
The timer on-delay is used to turn an output on or off after a preset amount of time has passed. You can see the required information in the instruction shown below.
The timer starts when the logic path preceding it goes from false to true. If the logic path transitions from true to false, the timer will be reset.

To determine the state of the timer, you can use a bit instruction on another rung. In this example, if the START switch is pressed in for 5 seconds, the LED attached to the output port module 0, position 0 will be turned on and remain on.......

Note that when your program starts after the processor changes mode, you may not know what condition your timer is in. Always check with the PLC manufacturer's documentation to know the initial states of the instructions...
The next instruction is the Timer Off-Delay (TOF) instruction. This instruction is very similar to that of the timer on-delay instruction.

The difference is that the timer is activated when the preceding logic goes from true to false and it resets when the preceding logic goes from false to true. All other aspects of this instruction are identical...
The last timing instruction is the Retentive Timer (RTO) instruction. This instruction has some similarities to the

This timer begins when the preceding logic makes a false to true transition; however, this will not reset the accumulator. The accumulator is reset with a reset instruction which will be covered later...

This is why this instruction is known as a retentive timer. It retains the accumulator value even when the timer is turned off. When timing resumes, it will begin at the count it had reached when the timer stopped...
Once the accumulator is past the preset value, the done bit will remain true until the reset instruction is used, regardless of the preceding logic.

This timer works similar to a recreational game. Suppose the length of the game is represented by the preset value. Low to high transitions represent when the game is in play, and high to low transition are time-outs...

During the game, the time-outs used do not take away from the total game time. During time-outs, the already elapsed time must be kept. When the game resumes, the time clock starts from where it left off...

Once the preset value is reached, the game is over. Regardless of what the teams are doing, low to high or high to low transitions, the game cannot continue. The reset instruction starts a new game...

There is one important item we have not discussed about timers. The timer instruction, when on, must be evaluated in a certain amount of time to be accurate. As your ladder logic loops, the time it takes to get back to the instruction again is important....
If the delay is too long, or you go to some long subroutine, then your timer can be incorrect and you have no way of knowing it. A typical maximum timer loop-time is 2.5 seconds.

Now that we have looked at the timing instructions, let's look at the counting instructions. There are three counting instructions. Again, the reset instruction is for both timer and counting instructions and will be covered last....

Counting instructions require a data file just as timer instructions do. This data file contains three words of 16 bits each. The first word, word 0, is the control word. The next word is the preset value. The last word is the accumulator value...
CU CD DN OU UN UA |
A counter can count both up and down. The direction depends on the instruction you use. Normally, the counter spans in range of -32,768 to 32,767 with zero being at the center....
When counting down, the processor stores the negative values as a two's complement number in the accumulator value location. Two's complement is a method of encoding negative numbers in binary...

Let's look at the different bits of the control word. The Counter Up Enable indicates that a count up instruction, which points to this counter data file, has a true logic path preceding the instruction...

The Counter Down Enable indicates that a count down instruction, which points to this counter data file, has a true logic path preceding the instruction. The done bit is set based on the accumulator value, preset values, and the instruction being used...
The overflow bit is set high when the accumulator counts beyond 32,767. This causes the processor to wrap around to
-32,768. To set this bit low, you must count down below -32,768 or use the reset instruction......

The underflow bit is set high when the accumulator counts down lower than -32,768 which causes the processor to wrap around to 32,767. To set this bit low, you must count up past 32,767 or use the reset instruction...
The last bit is the update accumulator, used by the high speed counter instruction. The usage of this bit will be covered later when we discuss the high speed counter instruction.

The first instruction we will look at is the Count Up (CTU) instruction. This instruction counts up for every false to true transition made by the preceding logic. The accumulator value is retained when the preceding logic is false...
When the counter accumulator value is equal to or greater than the preset value, the done bit is set high.
Remember, if the accumulator count goes higher than 32,767, the overflow bit will be set high. Also, when the preceding logic is high, the count up enable bit will be set high.

The next instruction we are going to look at is the Count Down (CTD) instruction. This instruction works almost identically to the count up instruction, only the accumulator is decremented on low to high transition...

The done bit is set low when the accumulator value is less than the preset value, and it is set high otherwise. If the count goes below -32,768, the underflow bit will be set high. When the preceding logic is true, the count down enable bit is also set in the control word of the counter data file...

The last type of counter instruction we are going to look at is the High-Speed Counter (HSC) instruction. This is a high speed version of the CTU instruction, which may not be implemented on all PLCs...
Some PLCs actually do the counting with hardware and just monitor it with software. Basically, the hardware counting is faster and counts from a predetermined input port.
As mentioned earlier, this instruction has the same parameters as the CDU instruction, but it is implemented in hardware instead of software.

The last instruction we are going to discuss is the Reset (RES) instruction. It is used to reset the accumulator and control bits of a timer, counter, or control instruction. Control instructions will be covered later in a separate lesson...

It is important to note that all timer and counter instructions can use the reset instruction EXCEPT the timer off-delay instruction. The timer off-delay instruction used with the reset instruction can cause unknown results...
The table below shows what is affected in each data file when the reset instruction is run. The data file to reset must be provided as a parameter to the instruction.
This lesson has examined the timing and counter instructions used by a typical PLC. These instructions are powerful when combined with bit instructions.
In the experiment, you will get a hands-on view of some of these instructions to see just how they operate.

1. The Timer On-Delay instruction is used to turn on or off a bit after a certain amount of time. A TON timer is enabled when the preceding logic makes a low to high transition. The accumulator and control bits are reset on a high to low transition.

2. The Timer Off-Delay instruction is also used to turn on or off a bit after a certain amount of time. A TOF timer is enabled when the preceding logic makes a high to low transition. The accumulator and control bits are reset on a low to high transition.

3. The Retentive Timer works the same as the timer on-delay; however, when the preceding logic path makes a high to low transition, the accumulator is not reset. When the timer is started again, it will start where it had left off.
4. The Count Up instruction increments its control data file's accumulator value for every low to high transition of the preceding logic path.
5. The Count Down instruction decrements its control data file's accumulator value for every low to high transition of the preceding logic path.
6. The High Speed Counter instruction is used for high speed counting. This instruction uses a hardware counter instead of a software counter.
7. The Reset instruction is used to reset the accumulator and control bits of timing, counting, and control instructions. This instruction is not to be used with the timer off-delay instruction...

The fifth rung waits for the second timer to finish. Once this timer has finished and sets the done bit to true, the LED is turned off and bit 1 of the PLC bit file is set back to high. This allows the first timer to start again as long as bit 0 is high...

The sixth rung contains the counter instruction. The reset instruction in rung 1 sets the accumulator to 1. Each low to high transition causes an increment in the counter data file accumulator value. The preset value is 5, so the done bit will be set when the counter (accumulator value) reaches 5...
The seventh rung checks to see when the final count is complete. After the done bit is set true, the unlatch instruction sets bit 0 of the bit data file to false or low.
